name: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
title: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
answer: Portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessment are three ways to capture what students know and can do beyond what a standard test measures. Portfolios show growth over time through collected work and student reflection, performance tasks ask students to apply knowledge to realistic problems, and oral assessment lets students explain their understanding aloud. Together they give a fuller picture of learning, while the teacher keeps the decisions that matter most.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Tests only capture part of what students know and can do, so this idea adds three complementary forms of assessment. A portfolio gathers work over time so growth becomes visible, and students can build digital portfolios with reflections on each piece. Performance tasks ask students to apply what they know to realistic problems, such as designing an experiment in science or building an argument from documents in history. Oral assessment lets students show understanding by explaining it, for example in a short recorded video about how they solved a problem. The problem it solves is the gap between what a test score shows and the fuller range of a student's knowledge and skills.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day practice, students assemble portfolios, often digital ones, and write reflections on each piece of work, while AI can help summarize patterns across the portfolio even though the student's own reflections carry the most meaning. Teachers design performance tasks, and AI tools can help draft the tasks and rubrics, but the teacher checks that the task measures the intended skills and is fair to all students. Oral assessment works by having a student explain their understanding, such as recording a short video on how they solved a problem, with recordings made on school devices and stored on school systems. The text does not give separate grade band guidance, so these practices are described for students generally rather than by year group. Across all three forms, the teacher remains the one who scores and judges the work.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It states plainly that tests capture only part of what students know and can do, and it describes portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessment as ways to show more. The one caution it offers is that automated scoring of speech can misjudge students with accents or developing language, which it attributes to Chapter 13. Beyond that, the idea rests on practice rather than research as presented here.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are set out clearly. AI can help summarize patterns across a portfolio, but the student's own reflections carry the most meaning, so the human voice is not replaced. AI can help draft performance tasks and rubrics, but the teacher must check that the task measures the intended skills and is fair to all students. Recordings for oral assessment should be made on school devices and stored on school systems, which keeps the work within school control. The teacher scores every oral assessment, because automated scoring of speech can misjudge students with accents or developing language. These decisions stay with a person, not with the tool.
